newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada offers U.S. a salmon catch counterproposal.
newsitem.headline: Canada offers U.S. a salmon catch counterproposal.

text.p: Canada made a new proposal to the United States on Monday in an attempt to reach an agreement to divide the Pacific salmon catch, a Canadian official said.

Chief Canadian negotiator Yves Fortier spoke with his U.S. counterpart, Mary Beth West, by telephone on Monday, responding to a U.S. offer made last week after three days of negotiations, Patricia Low-Bedard, a spokeswoman for Canada's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said.

Low-Bedard declined to provide details of the conversation, but a British Columbia government official said the latest offer represented a substantial change from the final Canadian position last week.
"It's a significant change," Dennis Brown, a special adviser to the provincial government on salmon issues, said.
Brown, who said British Columbia had not been consulted about the latest proposal, also declined to provide details.
The U.S. was expected to respond to Canada's proposal on Tuesday.

Talks broke down last week after both countries said the other was not willing to make the concessions necessary for a compromise. Canada called for the dispute to be resolved through binding third-party arbitration, an idea the United States rejected.
The two sides have squabbled for years on how to divide the Pacific salmon catch, and repeated attempts to negotiate a settlement have failed.
With the salmon season fast approaching, pressure had mounted to reach an agreement. At one point, the United States had threatened to begin fishing Canadian-bound salmon as early as this week.

The governments of Canada and British Columbia had threatened reprisals to pressure the United States into establishing fishing quotas. Canada announced last month that it would begin enforcing requirements that U.S. boats fishing in Canadian waters report to Canadian authorities. Under that policy, the Canadian Coast Guard temporarily seized four U.S. fishing boats.
British Columbia Premier Glen Clark, a vocal critic of the U.S. position, also announced plans to cancel a provincial lease on an underwater military testing site used by U.S. submarines.
